Automated written corrective feedback (AWCF) refers here to error feedback generated by software rather than by a teacher or peer, encompassing both dedicated automated writing evaluation (AWE) systems and large language models. This review synthesises the project library's evidence on AWCF for second-language writing, organised around three themes: detection accuracy relative to established tools, revision behaviour, and learner and teacher engagement. The library contains no controlled comparison of AWCF against teacher feedback on accuracy outcomes; the evidence is therefore drawn from corpus-based tool comparisons and naturalistic case studies.

Luo et al. (2025) compared ChatGPT-4 against Grammarly on 30 essays by non-English-major undergraduates at a Chinese university, analysing error flagging across three prompts. ChatGPT-4 maintained high precision across three prompts (94%, 98%, 94%), exceeding Grammarly's 85%, and with the most sophisticated prompt outperformed Grammarly on direct-translation, word-choice, sentence-structure and pronoun errors (Luo et al., 2025). Recall improved considerably across prompts, from 10% to 33% to 55% (Luo et al., 2025). The finding that a more sophisticated prompt did not reliably capture errors flagged by a simpler one further cautions against assuming prompt quality guarantees consistency (Luo et al., 2025). The design offers fine-grained error-category analysis but rests on 30 essays from intermediate-level learners at one Chinese institution, which the authors note limits generalisation (Luo et al., 2025).

Whether learners act on AWCF is a separate question from whether the tool detects errors. Naturalistic case evidence suggests that AWE tends to highlight rather than correct errors, whereas teacher feedback addressed more error types (Zhang & Hyland, 2018). The two focal learners differed sharply in resubmission frequency, and the more engaged learner improved more on both feedback sources (Zhang & Hyland, 2018). In a larger classroom case, 88% of 33 students submitted to AWE more than five times (Zhang & Hyland, 2021).

Teacher uptake is uneven: four of six teachers were positive about Grammarly, and no division of labour emerged in which the tool handled lower-order concerns (Koltovskaia, 2022). Reported time savings conflicted with observed feedback distribution (Koltovskaia, 2022). Hyland (2025) argues that ChatGPT's retiring stance leaves it unable to offer accurate feedback on rhetorical and pragmatic aspects of argument. These studies rely on small samples and hypothetical or single-context scenarios; none traces how teacher and automated feedback interact over time in an intact course.

sentences.sentence: ### 2.4 Synthesis and Research Gaps

Taken together, the library indicates that AWCF can match or exceed established tools on precision and on some error categories while remaining weaker on others, and that engagement with automated feedback varies widely across learners and teachers.

Three gaps follow: no library study compares AWCF with teacher feedback on accuracy in a controlled design; teacher–tool interaction has been examined only through one-time hypothetical scenarios (Koltovskaia, 2022); and prompt-design effects on learner revision outcomes remain untested.
These gaps motivate the present study's comparison of feedback conditions.

Evidence in this library on its accuracy, revision behaviour, and engagement is drawn from studies of Grammarly, an automated writing evaluation (AWE) system, and ChatGPT, and is organised around three themes: detection accuracy, revision and engagement, and teacher practice.
Comparative corpus work indicates that accuracy depends on the system and the error category.

ChatGPT-4 maintained high precision across three prompts (94%, 98%, 94%), exceeding Grammarly's 85%, and with the most sophisticated prompt outperformed Grammarly on direct-translation, word-choice, sentence-structure and pronoun errors (Luo et al., 2025).
The same study found that ChatGPT lagged behind Grammarly on article, preposition, spelling, verb-form and word-form errors (Luo et al., 2025).
Recall rose with prompt sophistication but remained modest, from 10% to 55% (Luo et al., 2025).

The design offers fine-grained error-category analysis but rests on 30 essays from intermediate-level learners at one Chinese institution, which the authors note limits generalisation (Luo et al., 2025).
The finding that a more sophisticated prompt did not reliably capture errors flagged by a simpler one further cautions against assuming prompt quality guarantees consistency (Luo et al., 2025).
Naturalistic case evidence suggests that AWE tends to highlight rather than correct errors, whereas teacher feedback addressed more error types (Zhang & Hyland, 2018).
The two focal learners differed sharply in resubmission frequency, and the more engaged learner improved more on both feedback sources (Zhang & Hyland, 2018).
The two-student design cannot separate feedback type from learner disposition.

In a larger classroom case, 88% of 33 students submitted to AWE more than five times, and integrated automated, peer and teacher feedback promoted behavioural, affective and cognitive engagement (Zhang & Hyland, 2021); the authors concede limited generalisability.
Peer-mediated revision involving Grammarly alongside self-reflection produced rubric gains between drafts (Li & Hebert, 2023), though a causal role for self-reflection was not established.
Teacher uptake is uneven: four of six teachers were positive about Grammarly, and no division of labour emerged in which the tool handled lower-order concerns (Koltovskaia, 2022).
Reported time savings conflicted with observed feedback distribution (Koltovskaia, 2022).
Concerns about AI's capacity to address rhetorical and pragmatic dimensions remain largely conceptual (Hyland, 2025).
No library study compares AWCF with teacher feedback on accuracy in a controlled design, and none examines whether prompt design alters learner revision outcomes.
Across themes, AWCF is accurate enough to flag many errors but uneven across categories, and engagement varies widely between learners.

Three gaps follow: no controlled comparison of AWCF and teacher feedback on accuracy; no evidence linking prompt sophistication to revision behaviour; and no naturalistic study of teacher–AWE division of labour.
These motivate the present demonstration.

The central assertion (ChatGPT's retiring stance → inability to offer accurate feedback on rhetorical/pragmatic aspects of argument) is stated in the same words with the same meaning, and the peripheral attribution of the "retiring" stance to ChatGPT's lower use of stance features is also supported ("the ChatGPT 4 essays ... contained a significantly lower frequency of features such as hedges, boosters, attitude markers, and self-mention"; "This leads to a more impersonal and expository tone"). No contradiction and no hedge removal.

uncited_sentences.sentence: Automated written corrective feedback (AWCF) refers here to error feedback generated by software rather than by a teacher or peer, encompassing both dedicated automated writing evaluation (AWE) systems and large language models.

This review synthesises the project library's evidence on AWCF for second-language writing, organised around three themes: detection accuracy relative to established tools, revision behaviour, and learner and teacher engagement.
The library contains no controlled comparison of AWCF against teacher feedback on accuracy outcomes; the evidence is therefore drawn from corpus-based tool comparisons and naturalistic case studies.
Accuracy of detection is the precondition for any downstream effect on writing.
Whether learners act on AWCF is a separate question from whether the tool detects errors.
These studies rely on small samples and hypothetical or single-context scenarios; none traces how teacher and automated feedback interact over time in an intact course.

Taken together, the library indicates that AWCF can match or exceed established tools on precision and on some error categories while remaining weaker on others, and that engagement with automated feedback varies widely across learners and teachers.
These gaps motivate the present study's comparison of feedback conditions.
